transcript: Lesson p3-pressure (Physics › Particle model of matter › Pressure in gases).
[check] OK: AI lesson opens by default (in TEACH_ENABLED) — AI lesson opened

T0: Welcome! Whenever you pump up a bike tyre or squeeze a balloon, you're seeing gas pressure, which comes from billions of tiny molecules zooming around randomly and crashing into the container's walls. What do you think the gas molecules are hitting that creates this pressure?
S1 (minimal): ok so what we doing

T1: We're working out where gas pressure comes from. Picture a balloon full of air: the gas molecules are zooming about and crashing into the inside of the balloon, and each crash pushes on it a tiny bit. What do you think we call each of those crashes?
S2 (minimal): what u mean by crashes

T2: Each of those crashes is called a collision, which is just a molecule striking the container wall. Every single collision gives the wall a tiny push, and huge numbers of them happen every second, which adds up to a steady pressure. So if a gas has far more collisions with the wall every second, what happens to the pressure?

T3: Fair enough, I'll keep it short. A collision is just one molecule hitting the wall, and each hit gives the wall a tiny push. If thousands more molecules hit the wall every second, what happens to the pressure?
T4: No worries if this is feeling confusing. Would you like me to just tell you the rest of this one?

T5: Gas molecules are always moving randomly, and their collisions with the walls make a steady pressure you can measure. The pressure pushes at right angles to the wall, and pressure = force ÷ area (Pa = N/m²). More or harder collisions mean higher pressure, so heating a gas in a fixed space makes molecules faster and the pressure rises, and squeezing it into less space means more collisions, so pressure rises too. Next: the temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of its molecules, so a hotter gas has faster molecules. If a gas gets hotter, what happens to the speed of its molecules?

T6: Got it, short version. Hotter gas means faster molecules, because temperature is linked to how much kinetic energy they have. So if you cool a gas right down, what happens to the speed of its molecules?

T7: Yes, slower is right: cooler gas means slower molecules. Now keep the gas in a sealed rigid container, so its volume stays the same (constant volume). If you heat it, the faster molecules hit the walls harder and more often. So what happens to the pressure?

T8: Yes, pressure goes up is right: faster molecules hit the walls harder and more often. Now keep the temperature constant and change the volume instead. If a gas is at 100 kPa and you squeeze it to half its volume, what is the new pressure?
S9 (wrong): um like 50 kpa? less space means less pressure right

T9: Not quite — 50 kPa is the wrong way round. Squeezing a gas into half the space makes the pressure go up, because the same molecules now hit the walls twice as often. So what is the new pressure when 100 kPa is squeezed to half its volume?

T10: Yes, 200 kPa is right: half the volume doubles the pressure. This pattern is called "inversely proportional" — when one quantity doubles, the other halves, so pressure × volume stays the same. So if you double the volume of a gas instead, what happens to its pressure?

T11: Not quite — it halves, not doubles. Inversely proportional means when the volume doubles, the pressure goes the opposite way. The same molecules now have twice the space, so they hit each part of the wall less often. So if a gas at 100 kPa has its volume doubled, what is the new pressure?

T12: Yes, 50 kPa is right: doubling the volume halves the pressure. Next idea: when you push a piston into a gas, you apply a force to it, and that is called doing work, which means transferring energy by a force. So when you push a bike pump handle in, what is being transferred to the air inside?

T13: Yes, energy is right: pushing the handle in transfers energy to the air. That energy adds to the gas's internal energy, which is the total kinetic and potential energy of all its molecules. So when you do work on a gas, what happens to its internal energy?

T14: Not quite: it goes up, not down. Pushing the handle in transfers energy to the air, so the total energy of its molecules increases. Think of the energy you put in as being added to what the air already had. If the internal energy of the air goes up, what happens to the temperature of the air in the pump?

T15: Yes, the temperature going up is right: doing work on the air raises its internal energy, so it warms up. That brings us to the end of this lesson. You answered questions on "Temperature and pressure at constant volume", "Pressure and volume at constant temperature" and "Doing work on a gas", and I explained "What causes gas pressure".
T16: Bye for now, and well done today! You can come back to this lesson any time you'd like to go over it again.
